findings.summary: the entry-point rule was installed at call-expression depth: a probe at the front of `compileCall`, which every call in every reached module goes through, so `x.catch(reporter)` ANYWHERE would drop its handler where before it was a source-located refusal. It is one rewrite of entry text in `entryStatements` now, beside the `main` form that erases the same wrapper by never treating it as entry text

because the rule sat below entry depth it could not set `hasMainEntry`, so scenes 200 and 201 generated a fidelity.json missing `entry-main-wrapper-erasure` -- the adaptation record the `main` form writes for exactly this erasure; both forms record it now
the refusal for a handler that is neither a report nor a recovery path was a generic unsupported-call error naming `catch`; at entry depth it names the entry contract the scene violated

the static `===` fold was a second `===`/`!==` lowerer in another module, while `compileCondition` already owns that operator with handle-identity, typed-data, static-string and static-number arms; the fold joins them, and is asked BEFORE the arms that would emit a comparison rather than after the ones that already did

`compileBoolean` returning an emitted comparison for an unsettled expression would have turned a refusal into a silent default at about a dozen callers that read its text as a decision -- the line family selects `useThinInstances`, `useVertexColor` and `depthWrite` on `=== "true"`; it delegates but takes only a settled answer, so every one of those keeps the located refusal

the browser-only-handler ladder was a verbatim copy of `compileDeferredCallback`'s own, 360 lines up the same file, and written as three arms where the concise-body and non-function cases are one `body ?? handler`; both sites share `isBrowserOnlyHandler` now

`statementIsBrowserOnly` looked like the deeper answer to reuse for that ladder and is not: it decides whether a statement inside a RETAINED function may be erased and deliberately excludes console and document, which is precisely what a reporter uses. Measured by trying it -- scene 200's own `console.error(err)` handler was refused. The reason is recorded where the choice is made

`crossGoldenMad` in the new test re-derived `compareImages` term for term -- the same mean-over-RGB-per-pixel metric every parity gate in the repo runs, in a repo whose audit lists 'one PNG/MAD library' among what is not worth re-deriving

the test restated four things the registry and the parity module already declare: the clear colour (a third copy of `backgroundColor`), a per-channel background tolerance of 8 where `compareRegion` answers the same question at the registry's declared threshold, and both golden paths the registry derives; all four are read rather than repeated

the cross-golden gate was in `test/corpus-goldens.test.ts`, whose one test is about golden APPLICATIONS and their manifest hashes; 200 and 201 are corpus scenes, so it moves to `test/corpus-scenes.test.ts` beside the manifest that carries their reference paths

a constraint BETWEEN two scenes' goldens is a new kind of evidence with no row in `docs/development.md`'s 'What a registered scene owns', so a recapture would follow that table and never learn a third file gates the pair; the table now names it

the reuse fix costs the test 24 ms of redundant PNG decodes (58 ms to 82 ms, measured) because `compareRegion(path, path, ...)` decodes the same file twice; kept, because it is 0.2% of a 34-second suite and buys four literals that can no longer drift from the registry

the probe's early-out cost was measured on the hot path before the move -- 7810 reaches on a doom compile, 46.8 ns each, 0.366 ms of a 3670 ms compile -- and the move to entry depth retires it to once per compile, so the reordering that would have recovered 0.14 ms is moot
